How model, colour and packaging set your minimum order

Why one total quantity is never the whole answer: how the model, colour split, logo versions, accessories, printed packaging and the mould decision each set the workable minimum — and how to plan a first order that stays simple.

A minimum is the smallest complete production plan, not a number

When a buyer asks for a minimum order quantity, the useful answer is not the smallest number we can type. It is the smallest order that can be run as one controlled plan: materials sourced, moulds allocated, decoration set up, components counted, packaging printed and goods inspected — all against a written specification.

One total quantity can hide many smaller batches. The same order split across several capacities, several colours and two logo versions is not one production group; it is several, and each has to be identified, decorated, counted and packed correctly. That is why we do not publish a category-wide figure on this site: it would describe an order that nobody actually places.

The product is only one layer. A printed box runs in its own economic quantities. A lid, an insert or an LED module is a separate supply line. A new colour needs approval and process control. A new mould is a development project that happens before any bulk output. Send the full breakdown and we can tell you which part of your project sets the practical minimum.

Route one: an existing model with limited variation

The most practical first order usually starts from a model that already exists. You pick a current body — a wine glass, a stopper, an ice bucket — and keep the first project to a clear specification: one or two colours, one logo file, one packaging format.

Every product page in our catalogue records the capacity, case pack, material and carton data for that model, so the discussion starts from a real body rather than a photograph. Existing models remove most of the product-development work, but they do not remove the need to confirm decoration and packaging; they simply give both sides something real to sample and measure.

Route two: decoration and accessories create their own minimums

A plain product and a finished private-label item are not the same order. Logo printing, colour coating or engraving each carry setup work and an approved sample. Several artwork versions divide the run into smaller groups. A lid, a sleeve, an insert or an LED module adds another supply line, and if the accessory colour changes, the order divides again.

These are the questions that decide it:

  • How many body models and capacities are involved?
  • How many colours, and how many pieces per colour?
  • How many logo files or logo colours, and what quantity per version?
  • Which accessories belong to each selling unit?
  • Does every item use the same pack structure?
  • Is it one shipment, or several destination-specific lots?

Route three: a new mould changes the conversation

We are a mould factory — the tooling is ours, and we run roughly two hundred new items a year. So when a buyer wants a shape that does not exist in the catalogue, the conversation is not about minimums at all; it is about a development project. Drawing review, tooling, trials and sample approval happen before any bulk production, and the economics of the order have to support that work.

A new mould makes sense when the shape creates real value: a protected brand silhouette, a functional improvement, a required dimension, or a collection you intend to reorder. If a current model meets the use and most of the visual goal, we will show you that route first — we would rather earn the reorder than sell the tooling.

When a supplier quotes a new shape at the same minimum and lead time as a catalogue item, check what is actually being promised. An existing model with decoration and a newly moulded body may share a product name, but they are not equivalent production plans.

Printed packaging is the hidden minimum

Packaging is usually the last detail a buyer sends and the first reason a small project becomes expensive. A plain export carton, a custom colour box and a rigid gift set are different materials, different setup and different run quantities. Inserts have to fit spouts, lids and accessories. Several language or barcode versions divide the packaging run even when the product is identical.

For a trial order we often recommend a standard protective structure with a simpler label or sleeve, then move to fully printed boxes once the assortment proves itself. The right answer depends on the channel: a retail buyer needs shelf information, an e-commerce seller needs parcel protection, and a venue buyer needs safe bulk handling more than a presentation box.

How we simplify a first order

A low-risk trial order is not a big assortment made small. It is a focused assortment designed to answer one commercial question. If the goal is to test demand, we usually recommend one existing shape, one or two capacities, fewer colours, one logo file and one packaging route. The first order then tells you which colour or capacity deserves the reorder.

We also keep sample quantity and bulk quantity separate. A sample exists to approve a product, a decoration or a pack; it does not prove that the same unit price applies to a small bulk run. Samples and bulk production are planned differently, and quoting them as if they were the same thing is how buyers end up comparing numbers that describe different orders.

Why a very small minimum inflates the unit price

Some setup work exists whether the order is large or small: artwork checking, decoration setup, packaging development, carton marks, sample approval and inspection planning. Spread that fixed work over fewer finished units and the unit price rises — that is arithmetic, not policy.

Freight distorts the comparison further. Drinkware is light but voluminous, so a small shipment still needs full protective cartons. Compare the total landed project — product, decoration, packaging, freight and destination charges — not the unit price alone. We would rather show you two clear routes, a simple one and a fully customised one, than quote a number that hides the difference.

Quality control does not become optional because the order is small

A trial order still needs a defined approval standard. We check goods against the confirmed model and the approved sample: capacity and dimensions where relevant, rim and finish, decoration, set count and carton protection. Small orders are more sensitive to error, not less, because there are fewer spare units and more variant splits to count. If four colours are packed into one set, counting accuracy is the difference between a saleable set and a return.

What to send before we can confirm a minimum

Send a short, specific brief and we will tell you which part of the project controls the minimum — and which change would make the first order easier to produce and repeat:

  • Product link, model number, drawing or reference photo
  • Target material and capacity
  • Total order quantity
  • Quantity per size, colour and logo version
  • Accessories or set components per selling unit
  • Retail, gift, e-commerce or bulk pack requirement
  • Destination country or warehouse
  • Target dispatch or launch date

Questions on this topic

Why don't you publish a minimum order quantity on each product page?

Because a single figure would describe an order nobody places. The workable minimum depends on the selected model, the colour split, the logo versions, the accessories and the packaging — all of which are configurable. We confirm it per project, in writing, against your full breakdown.

Request a quote

Does a custom colour change the minimum?

It can. What matters is the quantity per colour, not just the total. One colour across the whole order is one production group; four colours divide the run into four groups that each need process control, counting and packing.

Does adding a logo change the minimum?

Often yes. Each decoration process carries setup work and an approved first-off. One logo in one colour is a single group; several artwork versions or several logo colours divide the run again.

Does the packaging have its own minimum?

It can. Printed boxes, inserts and labels run in their own economic quantities, and language or barcode versions divide the run. We review product and packaging together so the minimum you receive describes the finished item, not the bare product.

Is the sample minimum the same as the bulk minimum?

No. A sample exists to approve a product, a decoration or a pack; it is planned and priced differently from bulk production. A sample proves the specification — it does not set the price of a small bulk run.

Can we start with a small test order?

Send your real target quantity and we will review it honestly. An existing model with limited customisation is the most realistic route, and we cannot promise that every project runs below its planning minimum. Simplifying capacities, colours, logos and printed packaging usually does more than negotiating the number.

How do we bring the minimum down?

Start from an existing model, hold one or two capacities, reduce the colour count, use one logo file and one pack structure. That keeps the order in the fewest production groups, and the first order then tells you which variant deserves the reorder.

Does a new mould raise the minimum?

A new mould is a development project — drawing review, tooling, trials and sample approval — priced separately from bulk production. The mould does not so much raise the minimum as change what the order has to support: it makes sense when the shape creates real value and you intend to reorder.

Another supplier quoted a lower minimum. Why?

Check what the two numbers describe. One may cover a plain product in bulk packing; the other a logo, a colour box and several colours. Compare the total landed project — product, decoration, packaging, freight and destination charges — and the specification each price is issued against.
